title: Exercise 4.1 — One workflow, two classifiers
text:
In Exercise 3.1 you predicted a number, blood glucose. Now the outcome is a class: will this person have a heart attack or a stroke in the next ten years, yes or no? The steps are exactly the same: specify a model, fit it on the training patients, and predict for new ones. Two things are new:

the specification says the model is for classification;
the prediction can be a probability for each class, as well as the class itself.










Exercise 3.1: glucose, a number
Exercise 4.1: an event, a class




specify (R)
linear_reg(), decision_tree() with set_mode("regression")
logistic_reg(), decision_tree() with set_mode("classification")


specify (Python)
LinearRegression(), DecisionTreeRegressor()
LogisticRegression(), DecisionTreeClassifier()


fit
fit() / .fit()
the same


predict
a number
a class, or a probability for each class




Part 1. Predict an event from age with a logistic regression. Get the probability and the class for one person, see the patient on the fitted curve, and compare the predictions with what was measured in the test patients.
Part 2. Add blood pressure and predict for the same person again. See the probability as a map over age and blood pressure.
Part 3. Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a decision tree instead. Follow the person to a leaf, read the probability and the class there, and compare the tree’s map with the logistic regression’s.







NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for the plots is folded away under Code for this plot (optional). You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you want it.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())

data/cvd_risk.csv holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check: their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and cvd, whether they had a cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years, yes or no. If you do not have it yet, download cvd_risk.csv into your data folder.

cvd <- read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv") |>
  mutate(cvd = factor(cvd, levels = c("no", "yes")))

summary(cvd)

#>       age         systolic_bp     cvd     
#>  Min.   :40.00   Min.   : 81.0   no :324  
#>  1st Qu.:49.00   1st Qu.:124.0   yes:176  
#>  Median :59.00   Median :135.5            
#>  Mean   :59.46   Mean   :135.8            
#>  3rd Qu.:69.00   3rd Qu.:147.2            
#>  Max.   :80.00   Max.   :189.0


The outcome is a factor with two levels, no then yes. The probabilities are then about yes: having an event.
We hold back every fifth person as the test set: 400 training patients and 100 test patients.

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(cvd), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- cvd[-test_rows, ]
test  <- cvd[test_rows, ]

count(train, cvd)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   cvd       n
#>   <fct> <int>
#> 1 no      258
#> 2 yes     142




Part 1 — Predict an event from age
The same three steps as in Exercise 3.1. The only change in the specification is the mode: classification instead of regression.

# 1. Specify: logistic regression, computed by glm(), for classification
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the weight for age
log_fit$fit$coefficients

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> -5.63801930  0.08321885


The two parameters are not on the probability scale but on the log-odds scale: an S-shaped function, the sigmoid, turns them into a probability. Here we let predict() do it.

Task 1a — A 70-year-old
predict() gives the class by default. With type = "prob" it gives a probability for each class instead.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
person <- data.frame(age = 70)

predict(log_fit, new_data = person, type = "______")   # a probability for each class
predict(log_fit, new_data = person)                     # the class







TipStuck?





The word in quotes is short for probability.



The class is the probability cut at 0.5: yes if \(\hat{P}(\text{yes}) > 0.5\), no otherwise. The red point is the 70-year-old, on the fitted curve:


Code for this plot (optional)
curve <- data.frame(age = seq(40, 80, by = 0.5))
curve$prob <- predict(log_fit, new_data = curve, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = train, aes(x = age, y = as.numeric(cvd == "yes")),
              width = 0.3, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.3, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(x = age, y = prob), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("point", x = 70,
           y = predict(log_fit, new_data = person, type = "prob")$.pred_yes,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Probability of an event",
       title = "Training patients (0 = no, 1 = yes), the fitted curve, and the 70-year-old")















ImportantThink about it




The model says yes for this person. How sure is it?
At about what age does the predicted class change from no to yes?





Task 1b — Predictions against what happened
The test patients were not used to fit the model. Predict both the probability and the class for each of them, and put them next to what happened.

test_results <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(log_fit, new_data = test))

head(test_results, 10)

#> # A tibble: 10 × 6
#>      age systolic_bp cvd   .pred_no .pred_yes .pred_class
#>    <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>    <dbl>     <dbl> <fct>      
#>  1    51         131 no       0.801     0.199 no         
#>  2    78         125 yes      0.299     0.701 yes        
#>  3    47         141 yes      0.849     0.151 no         
#>  4    63         146 yes      0.598     0.402 no         
#>  5    48         123 no       0.838     0.162 no         
#>  6    59         132 no       0.674     0.326 no         
#>  7    60         128 no       0.656     0.344 no         
#>  8    66         159 no       0.536     0.464 no         
#>  9    50         116 no       0.814     0.186 no         
#> 10    75         163 yes      0.354     0.646 yes




Code for this plot (optional)
ggplot(test_results, aes(x = age, y = .pred_yes, colour = cvd)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted probability of an event",
       colour = "What happened",
       title = "Test patients: predicted probability, coloured by what happened")















ImportantThink about it




Every point lies on the same curve. What has the model got wrong for the orange points below the dashed line, and for the blue points above it?
Which is more useful to a clinician: the class, or the probability?






Part 2 — Add blood pressure
The same specification, log_model, with a second predictor:

log_fit_2 <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

log_fit_2$fit$coefficients

#>  (Intercept)          age  systolic_bp 
#> -14.22258770   0.10415385   0.05291758



Task 2a — The same person, now with a blood pressure of 130

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
person <- data.frame(age = 70, systolic_bp = ______)

predict(log_fit_2, new_data = person, type = "______")
predict(log_fit_2, new_data = person)







TipStuck?





The person now needs a value for both predictors. Ask for the probabilities exactly as in Task 1a.



With two predictors, the probability is a map over age and blood pressure. The black line is where the probability is exactly 0.5: above it the class is yes, below it no. Circles are test patients without an event, triangles test patients with one, and the red point is the 70-year-old.


Code for this plot (optional)
# every combination of age and blood pressure on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(age = seq(40, 80, by = 0.5),
                    systolic_bp = seq(80, 200, by = 1))

prob_map <- function(fit, title) {
  grid$prob <- predict(fit, new_data = grid, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
  ggplot(grid, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = prob)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = prob), breaks = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = test, aes(shape = cvd), size = 1.5) +
    annotate("point", x = 70, y = 130, colour = "red", size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
    labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
         fill = "Probability\nof an event", shape = "Test patients", title = title)
}

prob_map(log_fit_2, "Logistic regression: age and blood pressure")















ImportantThink about it




The line where the class changes is straight but tilted. What does the tilt tell you?
Adding blood pressure moved this person from 0.547 to 0.487, and the class from yes to no. Did it change much about this person’s prediction?






Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree
Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the fit() and predict() calls stay the same.

# 1. Specify: a classification tree, computed by rpart
tree_model <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, extra = 106, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "BuOr", roundint = FALSE)








Each box asks a yes/no question. Yes goes left, no goes right. Each leaf at the bottom shows three things: the predicted class, the probability of yes (the share of training patients in that leaf who had an event) and the percentage of all training patients who ended up there.

Task 3a — Follow the person
Start at the top with the 70-year-old with a blood pressure of 130. At each question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach? What probability and what class does it give?
Check it with predict():

predict(tree_fit, new_data = person, type = "prob")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   .pred_no .pred_yes
#>      <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1    0.789     0.211

predict(tree_fit, new_data = person)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   .pred_class
#>   <fct>      
#> 1 no


The same map as for the logistic regression:


Code for this plot (optional)
prob_map(tree_fit, "Decision tree: age and blood pressure")















ImportantThink about it




The logistic regression gives every person their own probability. How many different probabilities can the tree give, and why?
Compare the two maps. What shape is the region where each model says yes?
The three models gave the 70-year-old 0.55, 0.49 and 0.21. What does that tell you?









ImportantLearning points




The steps are the same as in Exercise 3.1: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. For a class instead of a number, only the mode in the specification changes.
predict() gives the class; predict(type = "prob") gives a probability for each class. The class is the probability cut at 0.5.
The probability carries more information than the class: near 0.5 a small change flips the class.
A logistic regression’s probability changes smoothly and its classes are split by a straight line; a tree gives one probability per leaf and splits the classes into rectangles.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

data/cvd_risk.csv holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check: their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and cvd, whether they had a cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years, yes or no. If you do not have it yet, download cvd_risk.csv into your data folder.

cvd = pd.read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv")

cvd.describe()

#>              age  systolic_bp
#> count  500.00000   500.000000
#> mean    59.46400   135.752000
#> std     11.14887    18.066857
#> min     40.00000    81.000000
#> 25%     49.00000   124.000000
#> 50%     59.00000   135.500000
#> 75%     69.00000   147.250000

We hold back every fifth person as the test set: 400 training patients and 100 test patients.

is_test = cvd.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = cvd[~is_test]
test  = cvd[is_test]

train["cvd"].value_counts()

#> cvd
#> no     258
#> yes    142
#> Name: count, dtype: int64




Part 1 — Predict an event from age
The same three steps as in Exercise 3.1. The class name says that this model is for classification: LogisticRegression here, where Day 3 had LinearRegression.

# 1. Specify: logistic regression
log_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)

# 2. Fit on the training patients: predictors (a table) and outcome
log_model.fit(train[["age"]], train["cvd"])

On GitHub, the HTML representation is unable to render, please try loading this page with nbviewer.org.LogisticRegression?Documentation for LogisticRegressioniFitted
        
            
                Parameters
                










C  C: float, default=1.0

Inverse of regularization strength; must be a positive float.
Like in support vector machines, smaller values specify stronger
regularization. `C=np.inf` results in unpenalized logistic regression.
For a visual example on the effect of tuning the `C` parameter
with an L1 penalty, see:
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_logistic_path.py`.
inf




penalty  penalty: {'l1', 'l2', 'elasticnet', None}, default='l2'

Specify the norm of the penalty:

- `None`: no penalty is added;
- `'l2'`: add an L2 penalty term and it is the default choice;
- `'l1'`: add an L1 penalty term;
- `'elasticnet'`: both L1 and L2 penalty terms are added.

.. warning::
Some penalties may not work with some solvers. See the parameter
`solver` below, to know the compatibility between the penalty and
solver.

.. versionadded:: 0.19
l1 penalty with SAGA solver (allowing 'multinomial' + L1)

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`penalty` was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10.
Use `l1_ratio` and `C` instead. `l1_ratio=0` for `penalty='l2'`,
`l1_ratio=1` for `penalty='l1'`, `l1_ratio` set to any float between 0 and 1
for `penalty='elasticnet'`, and `C=np.inf` for `penalty=None`.
'deprecated'




l1_ratio  l1_ratio: float, default=0.0

The Elastic-Net mixing parameter, with `0 <= l1_ratio <= 1`. Setting
`l1_ratio=1` gives a pure L1-penalty, setting `l1_ratio=0` a pure L2-penalty.
Any value between 0 and 1 gives an Elastic-Net penalty of the form
`l1_ratio * L1 + (1 - l1_ratio) * L2`.

.. warning::
Certain values of `l1_ratio`, i.e. some penalties, may not work with some
solvers. See the parameter `solver` below, to know the compatibility between
the penalty and solver.

.. versionchanged:: 1.8
Default value changed from None to 0.0.

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`None` is deprecated and will be removed in version 1.10. Always use
`l1_ratio` to specify the penalty type.
0.0




dual  dual: bool, default=False

Dual (constrained) or primal (regularized, see also
:ref:`this equation <regularized-logistic-loss>`) formulation. Dual formulation
is only implemented for l2 penalty with liblinear solver. Prefer `dual=False`
when n_samples > n_features.
False




tol  tol: float, default=1e-4

Tolerance for stopping criteria.
0.0001




fit_intercept  fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Specifies if a constant (a.k.a. bias or intercept) should be
added to the decision function.
True




intercept_scaling  intercept_scaling: float, default=1

Useful only when the solver `liblinear` is used
and `self.fit_intercept` is set to `True`. In this case, `x` becomes
`[x, self.intercept_scaling]`,
i.e. a "synthetic" feature with constant value equal to
`intercept_scaling` is appended to the instance vector.
The intercept becomes
``intercept_scaling * synthetic_feature_weight``.

.. note::
The synthetic feature weight is subject to L1 or L2
regularization as all other features.
To lessen the effect of regularization on synthetic feature weight
(and therefore on the intercept) `intercept_scaling` has to be increased.
1




class_weight  class_weight: dict or 'balanced', default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one.

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
*class_weight='balanced'*
None




random_state  random_state: int, RandomState instance, default=None

Only used for `solver` == 'sag', 'saga' or 'liblinear' to shuffle the
data. It has no effect on the other solvers.
See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
None




solver  solver: {'lbfgs', 'liblinear', 'newton-cg', 'newton-cholesky', 'sag', 'saga'}, default='lbfgs'

Algorithm to use in the optimization problem. Default is 'lbfgs'.
To choose a solver, you might want to consider the following aspects:

- 'lbfgs' is a good default solver because it works reasonably well for a wide
class of problems.
- For :term:`multiclass` problems (`n_classes >= 3`), all solvers except
'liblinear' minimize the full multinomial loss, 'liblinear' will raise an
error.
- 'newton-cholesky' is a good choice for
`n_samples` >> `n_features * n_classes`, especially with one-hot encoded
categorical features with rare categories. Be aware that the memory usage
of this solver has a quadratic dependency on `n_features * n_classes`
because it explicitly computes the full Hessian matrix.
- For small datasets, 'liblinear' is a good choice, whereas 'sag'
and 'saga' are faster for large ones;
- 'liblinear' can only handle binary classification by default. To apply a
one-versus-rest scheme for the multiclass setting one can wrap it with the
:class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`.

.. warning::
The choice of the algorithm depends on the penalty chosen (`l1_ratio=0`
for L2-penalty, `l1_ratio=1` for L1-penalty and `0 < l1_ratio < 1` for
Elastic-Net) and on (multinomial) multiclass support:

================= ======================== ======================
solver l1_ratio multinomial multiclass
================= ======================== ======================
'lbfgs' l1_ratio=0 yes
'liblinear' l1_ratio=1 or l1_ratio=0 no
'newton-cg' l1_ratio=0 yes
'newton-cholesky' l1_ratio=0 yes
'sag' l1_ratio=0 yes
'saga' 0<=l1_ratio<=1 yes
================= ======================== ======================

.. note::
'sag' and 'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features
with approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with
a scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.

.. seealso::
Refer to the :ref:`User Guide <Logistic_regression>` for more
information regarding :class:`LogisticRegression` and more specifically the
:ref:`Table <logistic_regression_solvers>`
summarizing solver/penalty supports.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG) descent solver. Multinomial support in
version 0.18.
.. versionadded:: 0.19
SAGA solver.
.. versionchanged:: 0.22
The default solver changed from 'liblinear' to 'lbfgs' in 0.22.
.. versionadded:: 1.2
newton-cholesky solver. Multinomial support in version 1.6.
'lbfgs'




max_iter  max_iter: int, default=100

Maximum number of iterations taken for the solvers to converge.
100




verbose  verbose: int, default=0

For the liblinear and lbfgs solvers set verbose to any positive
number for verbosity.
0




warm_start  warm_start: bool, default=False

When set to True, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as
initialization, otherwise, just erase the previous solution.
Useless for liblinear solver. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
*warm_start* to support *lbfgs*, *newton-cg*, *sag*, *saga* solvers.
False




n_jobs  n_jobs: int, default=None

Does not have any effect.

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`n_jobs` is deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10.
None

print("classes:", log_model.classes_)

#> classes: ['no' 'yes']

#> intercept: [-5.63802661]

C=np.inf switches off a penalty that scikit-learn adds to logistic regression by default; without it the parameters would not match the ones in the R tab.
The two parameters are not on the probability scale but on the log-odds scale: an S-shaped function, the sigmoid, turns them into a probability. Here we let scikit-learn do it.

Task 1a — A 70-year-old
.predict() gives the class. .predict_proba() gives a probability for each class instead, one column per class in the order of classes_: no first, then yes.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
person = pd.DataFrame({"age": [70]})

print(log_model.______(person))   # a probability for each class: no, yes
print(log_model.predict(person))  # the class







TipStuck?





The method’s name is predict followed by an underscore and a short word for probability.



The class is the probability cut at 0.5: yes if \(\hat{P}(\text{yes}) > 0.5\), no otherwise. The red point is the 70-year-old, on the fitted curve:


Code for this plot (optional)
curve = pd.DataFrame({"age": np.arange(40, 80.5, 0.5)})
curve_prob = log_model.predict_proba(curve)[:, 1]
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(train["age"] + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, len(train)),
           (train["cvd"] == "yes") + rng.uniform(-0.03, 0.03, len(train)),
           alpha=0.3, color="steelblue")
ax.plot(curve["age"], curve_prob, color="red", linewidth=2)
ax.axhline(0.5, linestyle="--", color="grey")

In Exercise 4.1 the map of the logistic regression’s probability had a black line across it: to one side the model says yes, to the other no. That line is the decision boundary. Parts 1 and 2 use the same people as Exercise 4.1: age, systolic blood pressure, and whether they had a cardiovascular event in the next ten years. Both measurements matter, so the boundary is tilted.

Part 2. Change the threshold and see the line move: every threshold gives its own line.

Part 1 — Where the class changes
Fit a logistic regression with both measurements, the same way as in Exercise 4.1:

log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

b <- log_fit$fit$coefficients      # intercept, age, blood pressure
b

#>  (Intercept)          age  systolic_bp 
#> -14.22258770   0.10415385   0.05291758


The model is a straight line on the log-odds scale. Log-odds are another way of writing a probability \(p\): \(\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)\). A probability of 0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.
\[\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}\]
By default the model says yes when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5 the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and 0.5 for no event. Above it yes is the more likely class, below it no. So the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is log-odds of 0. So the boundary is every combination of age and blood pressure where
\[\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0\]
For a given blood pressure, solve for age:
\[\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}\]

Part 2 — The threshold moves the line
The cut-off of 0.5 is called the decision threshold. Nothing forces it to be 0.5: we could call someone yes from a probability of 0.3, or only from 0.7. A threshold \(t\) is a probability, so it has a log-odds, \(\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)\), and the boundary is where the model’s log-odds equal it:
\[\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)\]
Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves sideways. In the 3D plot of Part 1 this is cutting the S-shaped sheet at a different height: the 0.3 level meets it further down and to the left, the 0.7 level further up and to the right.

ImportantLearning points




The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal \(\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)\): 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
A logistic regression’s boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors. Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.

The model is a straight line on the log-odds scale. Log-odds are another way of writing a probability \(p\): \(\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)\). A probability of 0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.
\[\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}\]
By default the model says yes when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5 the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and 0.5 for no event. Above it yes is the more likely class, below it no. So the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is log-odds of 0. So the boundary is every combination of age and blood pressure where
\[\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0\]
For a given blood pressure, solve for age:
\[\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}\]

Part 2 — The threshold moves the line
The cut-off of 0.5 is called the decision threshold. Nothing forces it to be 0.5: we could call someone yes from a probability of 0.3, or only from 0.7. A threshold \(t\) is a probability, so it has a log-odds, \(\log\big(t / (1 - t)\big)\), and the boundary is where the model’s log-odds equal it:
\[\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = \log\left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)\]
Only the right-hand side changes, so the line keeps its tilt and moves sideways. In the 3D plot of Part 1 this is cutting the S-shaped sheet at a different height: the 0.3 level meets it further down and to the left, the 0.7 level further up and to the right.

ImportantThink about it




Look at the straight-line model’s map. Does it ever say yes?
The straight-line model says sodium hardly matters. Is that true?
Describe the boundary of the model with the squared term, and of the tree.









ImportantLearning points




The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the threshold. For a logistic regression that is where the log-odds equal \(\log\big(t/(1-t)\big)\): 0 for a threshold of 0.5.
A logistic regression’s boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors. Changing the threshold moves it without changing its tilt.
When the risk is high at both ends of a measurement, no straight line can separate the classes, and a weight near 0 can hide a strong relationship.
A boundary can bend if you give the model a curved predictor, such as a squared term, or use a model that bends on its own, such as a tree.

Stretch
In Exercise 4.2 every threshold gave a different line, and 0.5, where both classes are equally likely, was only the default. Why would anyone move it? This exercise answers that question, back on one measurement, age.
A logistic regression outputs a probability,
\[\hat{p}(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid x),\]
but a clinic needs a decision: offer this person treatment to prevent a heart attack or stroke, or not. To turn the probability into a predicted class we choose a decision threshold. Usually:
But 0.5 is arbitrary. Changing the threshold changes how many true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives the model makes, and so which mistakes it makes.
Theory: decision threshold; confusion table; true and false positives and negatives; sensitivity and specificity; why you would move the threshold.
